sources.name: The Stargate Collection - CIA Program on Remote Viewing

desc: STAR GATE is the umbrella name applied in 1991 to a chain of United States government programmes investigating and attempting to operationalise remote viewing, running from 1970 to 1995 across CIA, Army and DIA sponsorship. The CIA initiated SCANATE - 'scan by coordinate' - around 1970 in response to assessments that the Soviet Union was spending heavily on psychotronic research. In 1972 physicists Harold E. Puthoff and Russell Targ began CIA-sponsored work at SRI International's Artificial Intelligence Center in Menlo Park, coining the term 'remote viewing' and working with Ingo Swann, Pat Price, Joseph McMoneagle and Uri Geller. The military side began as GONDOLA WISH in 1977 under the Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence's Systems Exploitation Detachment, became GRILL FLAME under INSCOM in mid-1978 in Buildings 2560-2561 at Fort Meade, was redesignated CENTER LANE in 1983, moved to DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate as SUN STREAK in late 1985, and was consolidated as STAR GATE in 1991. Maj. Gen. Albert Stubblebine sponsored the Fort Meade effort; Lt. Frederick 'Skip' Atwater oversaw the unit until 1987; James Clapper, later Director of National Intelligence, led the project in the 1990s; Edwin C. May ran the Cognitive Sciences Laboratory as principal investigator. In 1995 CIA commissioned the American Institutes for Research to evaluate the programme; statistician Jessica Utts concluded the laboratory results showed statistically significant effects, psychologist Ray Hyman concluded the opposite - 'the overwhelming amount of data generated by the viewers is vague, general, and way off target' - and the official finding was that remote viewing information 'is vague and ambiguous, making it difficult, if not impossible, for the technique to yield information of sufficient quality and accuracy for actionable intelligence.' CIA terminated the roughly $20 million programme in 1995 and published the records online in January 2017 through the CREST archive; Edwin May's donated 1972-1995 materials are held at the Archives of the Impossible at Rice University. STAR GATE belongs on this board for four reasons and only four. It is a documented case of the United States funding two decades of research into a phenomenon it publicly disparaged. It shows the exact contractor structure a concealed programme uses - a university-adjacent institute holding the science, a compartmented military unit holding the operations, and an intelligence sponsor holding the money. It establishes the personnel bridge that runs through Puthoff from SRI to EarthTech to the AAWSAP Defense Intelligence Reference Documents to To The Stars Academy and the 2019 Army CRADA, and through Christopher 'Kit' Green from the CIA weird desk to NIDS-adjacent biomedical work. And it is the precedent for how such a programme ends: not with a public admission, but with a commissioned evaluation that produces an unusable-for-intelligence finding, followed by termination and, twenty-two years later, bulk declassification.

claims.text: A SECRET CIA memorandum titled 'Star Gate - Program Status and Proposed New Direction' records that a Congressionally Directed Action transferred the STAR GATE program to CIA, that the Executive Director approved CIA's recommended approach in late January 1995, and that the approach was 'formally transmitted to Congress and briefed to Richard D'Amato of the SAC staff on 27 March 1995.'

The same CIA memorandum states that CIA 'have been working closely with DIA and their support contractor to identify all relevant documents pertaining to Star Gate and have made plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program' - meaning the scope of the eventual public release was decided before the outside evaluation was performed.

The same CIA memorandum records that the National Research Council declined to perform the evaluation by letter dated 5 May 1995, and that CIA was then referred to Dr. David Goslin, President of the American Institutes for Research.

The same CIA memorandum recommends terminating before the review is performed: 'I recommend we adopt this alternative plan and ask Congress to agree that the program should NOT be transferred to CIA,' noting that even if AIR proceeded 'there exists a very strong possibility that AIR will merely reach the same conclusion firmly held by the NRC.'

The same CIA memorandum states that 'neither the DO nor the DI were at all interested in having this program reside in their directorates,' and that a decision on the operational personnel then at DIA was deferred pending the blue-ribbon panel assessment.

The American Institutes for Research final report, 'An Evaluation of Remote Viewing: Research and Applications,' is dated 29 September 1995 and was released to the public on 28 November 1995; its final recommendation was to terminate the STAR GATE effort.

STAR GATE was the last in a chain of renamed programs: SCANATE (CIA-funded from 1970), GONDOLA WISH (Army ACSI Systems Exploitation Detachment, 1977), GRILL FLAME (Army INSCOM 'Detachment G,' buildings 2560 and 2561 at Fort Meade, mid-1978), INSCOM CENTER LANE Project (1983), SUN STREAK (DIA Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate, office code DT-S, late 1985), STAR GATE (1991).

In 1991 the program transitioned to Science Applications International Corporation (SAIC) and was changed from a Special Access Program to a LIMDIS (limited dissemination) program; Edwin May presided over 70 percent of the total contractor budget and 85 percent of the program's data collection.

Remote viewing research began in 1972 at Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, California, conducted by Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff, initially focused on a small number of individuals including Ingo Swann.

Over more than two decades roughly $20 million was spent on STAR GATE and related activities, with about $11 million budgeted from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s; over forty personnel served in the program at various times, including about twenty-three remote viewers.
The FY1995 Defense Appropriations bill directed that the program be transferred to CIA and that CIA conduct a retrospective review of it.
The program's political survival depended on two named legislators: Senator Claiborne Pell (D-RI) and Representative Charles Rose (D-NC).

The existence of the then-highly-classified program was publicly reported by columnist Jack Anderson in April 1984; a 1984 National Academy of Sciences / National Research Council evaluation performed for the Army Research Institute returned unfavorable results.

The AIR evaluation contained a positive assessment by statistician Jessica Utts finding a statistically significant laboratory effect, offset by a negative assessment by psychologist Ray Hyman; CIA's public conclusion was that there was no case in which ESP had provided data used to guide intelligence operations.

DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate (DT-S) hosted the program from 1985 to 1991; DIA is the same agency that later hosted AAWSAP, making DIA the most persistent institutional host across both threads.

The pattern of serial renaming and inter-agency transfer is the template the board applies to the alleged legacy recovery program; STAR GATE is the control case where the template is documented rather than inferred.

American Institutes for Research and its president David Goslin are the named third-party validators used to close the program, the same 'independent review' device later used with the NASA 2023 UAP study panel and AARO's Historical Record Report.
dossier.denialPosture: CIA's public position at termination was that remote viewing had never produced data used to guide an intelligence operation and that the program was scientifically unsupported, a verdict delivered through a contracted outside evaluator rather than in CIA's own voice. The 1995 internal memorandum shows that position was arrived at before the evaluation was contracted, and that the declassification package was scoped in parallel by CIA and DIA to exclude 'the most sensitive aspects of the program.'
dossier.narrative:
The origin story is threat-mirroring. Between 1969 and 1971, U.S. intelligence concluded the Soviet Union was investing seriously in what it called psychotronics, with estimates running to 60 million rubles per year by 1970 and over 300 million by 1975. Whether or not the Soviets had anything, the money itself was treated as evidence, and CIA opened a research line in 1970 under the name SCANATE. In 1972 the research moved to Stanford Research Institute in Menlo Park, where Russell Targ and Harold Puthoff ran it, initially around a small set of gifted individuals including the artist Ingo Swann. The client requirement, per the FAS program file, was a minimum accuracy of 65 percent.

The operational side grew separately out of the Army. GONDOLA WISH, a 1977 Army Assistant Chief of Staff for Intelligence effort under the Systems Exploitation Detachment, was chartered to evaluate potential adversary applications of remote viewing. It became a collection project in mid-1978 as GRILL FLAME, INSCOM 'Detachment G,' housed in buildings 2560 and 2561 at Fort Meade, Maryland. The SRI research was folded into GRILL FLAME in early 1979, and hundreds of experiments were run at SRI through 1986. Renamed the INSCOM CENTER LANE Project in 1983, the unit adopted a written methodology developed by Swann and Puthoff meant to make the capability trainable rather than innate. Its existence surfaced publicly when columnist Jack Anderson reported on it in April 1984. That same year the National Academy of Sciences' National Research Council evaluated remote viewing for the Army Research Institute and returned an unfavorable verdict. When Army funding ended in late 1985, the unit did not die; it was redesignated SUN STREAK and moved to DIA's Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate under office code DT-S. In 1991 the contract moved to Science Applications International Corporation and the program became STAR GATE, downgraded from a Special Access Program to a LIMDIS, limited dissemination, program. Edwin May presided over roughly 70 percent of the total contractor budget and 85 percent of data collection. Over two decades the effort consumed on the order of $20 million, with about $11 million spent from the mid-1980s to the early 1990s, and involved more than forty personnel including about twenty-three remote viewers.

The end is where the concealment mechanics are legible. The FY1995 Defense Appropriations bill directed transfer to CIA and directed CIA to conduct a retrospective review. What happened next is documented in a SECRET memorandum, 'Star Gate - Program Status and Proposed New Direction,' now in the CIA reading room as CIA-RDP96-00791R000100160001-0. The Executive Director approved CIA's approach in late January 1995; it was transmitted to Congress and briefed to Richard D'Amato of the Senate Appropriations Committee staff on 27 March 1995. CIA transferred funds to the Army Research Institute to make it executive agent for a National Research Council blue-ribbon review. In parallel, and this is the sentence that matters for the board, CIA was 'working closely with DIA and their support contractor to identify all relevant documents pertaining to Star Gate' and had 'made plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program.' The sorting of what the public would eventually see was underway before the verdict was in.

NRC declined the review by letter dated 5 May 1995, citing its own 1988 report and quoting its conclusion that the case for remote viewing was 'not just very weak, but virtually nonexistent.' NRC referred CIA to Dr. David Goslin, president of the American Institutes for Research. The memo's author then recommended skipping the review entirely: 'in view of the strong position taken by the NRC... I want to propose at this point that we strongly consider the option of going back to Congress with the recommendation not to accept the Star Gate program from DIA,' adding that even if AIR proceeded 'there exists a very strong possibility that AIR will merely reach the same conclusion firmly held by the NRC.' He also recorded that 'neither the DO nor the DI were at all interested in having this program reside in their directorates,' and deferred any decision about the operational personnel still at DIA. The recommendation was explicit: 'ask Congress to agree that the program should NOT be transferred to CIA.'

AIR did the review anyway. Its final report is dated 29 September 1995 and was released publicly on 28 November 1995. It contained two irreconcilable assessments, statistician Jessica Utts finding a statistically significant laboratory effect and psychologist Ray Hyman finding none, and a single recommendation to terminate. CIA's public line was that there was no case in which ESP had provided data used to guide intelligence operations. The program had been sustained politically for years by Senator Claiborne Pell of Rhode Island and Representative Charles Rose of North Carolina; with the program dead, the constituency dissolved.

What the board should take from STAR GATE is not whether remote viewing worked. It is the demonstrated administrative repertoire: serial renaming across host commands, movement between Army, DIA and CIA, SAP-to-LIMDIS reclassification, contractor intermediation, a pre-cooked termination decision, a curated declassification, and a public verdict framed in the language of science rather than of budget politics. Every one of those moves is available to any program that wants to disappear while remaining funded, and every one is documented here in the government's own paper.

dossier.whatItIs: STAR GATE was the final code name for a U.S. government psychic-intelligence effort that ran from roughly 1970 to 1995 under a rotating series of names and host agencies: SCANATE (CIA-funded, from 1970), GONDOLA WISH (Army ACSI, 1977), GRILL FLAME (Army INSCOM Detachment G at Fort Meade, 1978), INSCOM CENTER LANE (1983), SUN STREAK (DIA Scientific and Technical Intelligence Directorate, office code DT-S, 1985), and STAR GATE (DIA with SAIC as prime contractor, 1991). It combined an operational collection unit that tasked trained remote viewers against real intelligence targets with a separately maintained contract research program run out of Stanford Research Institute. It was terminated in 1995 after a Congressionally Directed Action moved it to CIA and CIA declined to keep it.
dossier.whyImplicated: STAR GATE is the board's cleanest declassified proof-of-concept for the exact institutional pattern the legacy program is alleged to follow: a real, funded, operational, compartmented effort into a phenomenon the government publicly treated as nonsense, sustained across two decades and at least four host organizations by serial renaming, moved between Army, DIA and CIA in a way that defeats continuity of oversight, and run through a cleared contractor (SRI, then SAIC) rather than in-house. The 1995 CIA program-status memorandum shows the disposal mechanics with unusual clarity: CIA and DIA had already made 'plans to declassify all but the most sensitive aspects of the program' before any evaluation was complete, and the memo's author recommended asking Congress to agree the program should NOT transfer to CIA before the contracted review had even begun. That is a decision to terminate reached in advance of the evidence, followed by a curated declassification, which means the archive the public got is the residue of a deliberate sorting operation rather than a data dump. The program also demonstrates that a phenomenon-adjacent effort could be carried in the black for twenty-five years while officials denied its existence, and that its closure could be framed publicly as a scientific verdict rather than a bureaucratic one. Finally, STAR GATE is a personnel bridge: the scientists, contractors and case officers it credentialed are the same names that reappear in the NIDS, AAWSAP and To The Stars-era record, giving the board a documented lineage from Cold War compartmented research to the 2017-2026 disclosure fight.
